rv.q: A fine ensemble is anchored by a standout performance from Duff.

Gripping, subtle performances power this revival of Lillian Hellman’s pungent portrait of a wealthy family torn apart by rampant greed Written in 1939, Lillian Hellman’s Deep South-set drama remains a compelling, satisfyingly twisty thriller of unrestrained greed and dysfunctional family dynamics.

Now they are set to strike a deal with a Chicago businessman to build a local mill that will make them millionaires. When their estranged, gravely ill brother-in-law Horace (John Light) refuses the final essential backing, Benjamin and Oscar (Mark Bonnar and Steffan Rhodri, different shades of nasty and both excellent) plot a scheme to trick him.
Confusing design quirks aside, it’s a chic and steely revival of a play that is both fascinating and (understandably) rarely done.
Still, this production’s uneven performances and dour staging don’t make a particularly seductive case for revisiting it.
Duff is the best of a classy pack.
For all the excellence of the performances, Lyndsey Turner’s production stubbornly refuses to coalesce into a compelling whole...
The Young Vic sorely needs a big hit; but this isn’t it.
Just in time for Christmas, this is a tasty but cheerless exercise in family feuds.
In The Little Foxes, the design by Lizzie Clachan is at war with Lillian Hellman's play.
That, sadly, turned out to be the dramatic high point of the evening.

The Young Vic’s somewhat surprising Christmas offering is Lillian Hellman’s 1939. Southern States family drama THE LITTLE FOXES (a title suggested to her by Dorothy Parker purportedly taken from the biblical Song of Solomon). The play first appeared on Broadway with Tallulah Bankhead and later as a film starring Bette Davis.

Everyone is miserable in this house, where children become pawns in their parents’ gross games to keep wealth in the family, and women are told a frown never got them anywhere. Duff’s Regina and Worthington-Cox’s Alexandra share a painful final scene, yet there’s no real sense of redemption, which makes this a hard watch.
On the evidence of the Young Vic’s new production, that’s both a shame and understandable.
It's a case of not being more than the sum of its parts, even if those parts are well constructed and polished.

cn.t: Critics are split on this Young Vic revival: Duff's performance earns consistent praise, but Turner's heavy-handed direction divides opinion on whether it serves or smothers Hellman's razor-sharp family drama.
